tip: The suffix '-nya' can mean 'the one we know': 'deadline-nya besok' = the deadline is tomorrow.
'Tinggal' usually means live or stay, but here it means remaining: 'waktu kita tinggal dua hari' = we only have two days left. Context decides which 'tinggal' you've met.
'Mohon maaf' = formal apology, softer than plain 'maaf': 'mohon maaf, laporan saya terlambat satu hari' = my apologies, my report is one day late.
'Jauh-jauh hari' is literally 'far-far days' – doubling 'jauh' stretches the distance in time, giving 'well in advance': 'ajukan jauh-jauh hari'.
'Mohon izin' = formal 'I request permission': 'saya mohon izin cuti' = I request leave.
'Yang' marks who does it: 'Rina yang menggantikan saya' = it's Rina who covers for me.
'Cuti bersama' = collective leave the whole office takes at once: 'cuti bersama tahun ini' = this year's collective leave.
'Masuk' literally means enter, but on its own it often means coming in to work or school: 'saya tidak bisa masuk' = I can't come in. 'Tidak masuk' is the usual way to say absent.
'Badan tidak enak' = feeling unwell (lit. body not nice): 'kalau badan tidak enak' = if you're feeling unwell.
'Melamar kerja' = to apply for a job – 'melamar' alone can also mean to propose marriage!
Interviewers normally use 'Anda', not 'kamu': 'pengalaman kerja Anda' = your work experience.
Bare 'kerja' is any work; add '-nya' and it's this specific one: 'kerjanya juga berat' = the work is also heavy. Here '-nya' does the job of English 'the'.
Doubling a verb often softens it: 'pikir-pikir' = mull it over for a while.
In thanks, 'atas' = for: 'terima kasih atas kesempatan wawancara ini' = thank you for this interview opportunity.
'Biar saya yang...' = let me be the one to...: 'biar saya yang balas' = let me reply.
'Sungkan' isn't plain hesitation – it's the feeling of not wanting to impose on someone. 'Jangan sungkan bertanya' = don't hold back out of politeness, just ask.
'Saling' before a verb makes it mutual: 'membantu' = help, 'saling membantu' = help each other. No extra 'each other' word needed after the verb.
'Pinjam' = borrow; 'meminjamkan' = lend (the 'p' melts into 'm' after 'me-'): 'dia meminjamkan payungnya' = she lent her umbrella.
The ending '-kan' can add 'for someone': 'bawa' → 'membawakan saya kopi' = bring me coffee.
'Minta tolong' = ask a favor: 'boleh saya minta tolong?' = may I ask a favor?
'Tanda tangan' = signature (lit. hand mark): 'perlu tanda tangan' = needs a signature.
'Salah' + verb = do it wrong: 'salah kirim' = sent to the wrong place.
Verb + 'ulang' = do it again: 'kirim ulang' = re-send it.
'Mohon' + verb = very polite request, softer than 'tolong': 'mohon periksa' = please check.
'Akhirnya ... juga' = finally, at last: 'akhirnya proyek kami selesai juga' = our project is finally done.
Indonesians use English 'check-in' as-is at airports and hotels: 'kami harus check-in' = we have to check in.
'Anda' (capital A) is the polite you that staff use with strangers: 'paspor dan tiket Anda' = your passport and ticket.
The suffix '-nya' can turn a describing word into a noun: 'berat' = heavy, 'beratnya' = its weight.
Indonesian often puts the object first: 'tas kecil ini saya bawa' = this small bag I'll take. The doer comes right after it, with no extra words needed.
'Tolong' literally means help, and it turns a command into a polite request: 'tolong taruh koper Anda' = please put your suitcase.
